title: Inequality, Part 1: The New Deal's Raw Deal
author: Terry Underwood
source: Learning to Read, Reading to Learn on Substack, December 19, 2025
summary: The New Deal produced profoundly unequal outcomes across racial and regional lines, though this is often obscured by its celebration for ending the Depression. Many programs explicitly excluded Black workers or relegated them to the least desirable positions. Agricultural support benefited large landowners while displacing tenant farmers, who were disproportionately Black in the South. Northern industrial workers and union members gained substantial protections and public employment, while Black workers, especially in the South, saw fewer protections and more displacement. This pattern was not accidental but structural, reflecting how Southern Democratic negotiators shaped federal programs to preserve existing racial hierarchies. Understanding the New Deal's distributional reality is critical for recognizing how policy negotiations with powerful state actors embed inequality.
points: Policy design embeds inequality: The New Deal's racial disparities were not bugs but features, shaped by Southern negotiators who wielded political power.
Exclusion was structural: Many programs explicitly excluded Black workers or placed them in the least desirable positions, not accidentally but by design.
Regional power shapes distribution: Northern industrial workers and union members gained substantially; Southern Black workers saw displacement and fewer protections.
Contemporary lessons about negotiation: When large social programs are negotiated with powerful local actors, those actors will shape distribution to reflect their interests.
quotes: The New Deal is celebrated as a turning point in American social policy, yet its actual effects were deeply unequal across racial and regional lines.

Many New Deal programs explicitly excluded Black workers or placed them in the least desirable positions. Agricultural programs benefited large landowners while displacing tenant farmers and agricultural laborers.
The pattern was not accidental. The New Deal was negotiated between the federal government and state actors, particularly Southern Democrats, who shaped programs to preserve existing hierarchies.
When large social programs are negotiated with powerful state and local actors, those actors shape distribution according to their interests.

Understanding the New Deal's distributional reality is critical for understanding how policy creates inequality and how contemporary policies might be more attentive to whose interests are served.” Archived from Learning to Read, Reading to Learn on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
